package com.myapp.adventure.engine.ir

import com.myapp.adventure.engine.ir.types.VarDecl
import kotlinx.serialization.SerialName
import kotlinx.serialization.Serializable

/**
 * Ф4.1: a reusable choice template — an authoring entity that can be
 * instantiated in many scenes with different parameter values.
 *
 * **Status (Ф4.1).** AST-only. Parsed from JSON into
 * `Adventure.choiceTemplates`, but not yet instantiated into a
 * `Choice`. Instantiation lands in Ф4.2 (`applyTemplate(templateId,
 * args)`). Until then, `Adventure.choiceTemplates` is parsed
 * infrastructure with no consumer — a `Choice` in any scene still has
 * its own `text` / `condition` / `effects`.
 *
 * **Why a template.** Suppose three scenes have a "Use potion" choice:
 * same text, same effect (`potion: -1`, `health: +20`), same
 * availability (`potion > 0`), same target (back to the current scene).
 * Without a template, the author duplicates five fields across three
 * scenes, and any change (e.g. `potion: -2` instead of `-1`) must be
 * repeated in every copy — easy to miss one.
 *
 * A `ChoiceTemplate` is the single source of truth; a scene uses it via
 * `Choice.templateRef` (Ф4.2) and provides only the args
 * (`{"itemId": "potion", "quantity": 1}`).
 *
 * **Not bound to a scene.** A template is declared once at the adventure
 * level (`Adventure.choiceTemplates`) and can be used by any number of
 * scenes, any number of times. This is the "reusable" part of "reusable
 * choice template".
 *
 * **Not checked by TypeChecker today.** `TypeChecker.check` walks
 * `Adventure.chapters` only. Templates are skipped in Ф4.1 — their
 * conditions reference parameters (`itemId`, `quantity`) that are not in
 * `Adventure.variables`, and checking them against the global scope
 * would produce false `UnknownVariable` errors. Ф4.2.2 (a follow-up sub-step) will extend `TypeChecker` with a `checkChoiceTemplate(template, globalVariables)` that builds a combined scope (`parameters + globalVariables`) and runs the same checks.
 *
 * @property id unique identifier within `Adventure.choiceTemplates`.
 *   Duplicates are a `ParseError.Structure` (checked by `JsonToIr`).
 *   Referenced by `Choice.templateRef` in Ф4.2.
 * @property parameters typed parameter declarations. Each `VarDecl` has
 *   a `name` (unique within the template) and a `VarType`. The parameter
 *   type participates in the template's own type-scope: a
 *   `Compare("itemId", GT, 0)` in `visibilityCondition` must resolve
 *   `itemId` to the declared type. Type-checking of templates lands in
 *   Ф4.2 (the `TypeChecker` extension needs to know the local scope;
 *   today it only knows `Adventure.variables`).
@property text literal display string. **Ф4.2:** `{paramName}` placeholders are substituted by `applyTemplate`; the substitution syntax (`{paramName}`) was decided in Ф4.2.1 (see `docs/engine-architecture.md` §"Choice templates"). Verbatim when no placeholders are present.
 * @property visibilityCondition when to **show** the choice. `null` =
 *   always visible. Distinct from `availabilityCondition` (below); the
 *   reader (N4 / Ф4.4) shows a hidden choice **not at all**, but shows
 *   an unavailable choice **disabled**, with a reason. The two-condition
 *   split is the AST-level support for N4; Ф4.4 implements the UI
 *   behaviour.
 * @property availabilityCondition when the choice is **clickable**.
 *   `null` = always clickable (subject to `visibilityCondition` being
 *   shown). This is the role that `Choice.condition` plays today in the
 *   reader; Ф4.4 will split it into two at the `Choice` level too.
 * @property effects applied when the choice is picked, in list order.
 *   Same `Effect` model as `Choice.effects`.
@property nextScene target scene. Two kinds of value:
- a normal `SceneId` — fixed target, copied as-is on instantiation;
- [SELF] (`SceneId("@self")`) — "the scene where this template is
applied". Resolved by `applyTemplate` from its `currentSceneId`
argument. The canonical case is "use item" / "drink potion": the
choice does not move the player to a different scene, it applies
effects in place. `@` cannot appear in a real scene id (the editor
strips it in `transliterate`), so there is no collision. A
non-template `Choice` with `next_scene: "@self"` is an ordinary
dangling reference (`CompileError.MissingNextScene`) — `@self` is a
template-only marker.
 */
@Serializable
public data class ChoiceTemplate(
    public val id: String,
    public val parameters: List<VarDecl> = emptyList(),
    public val text: String,
    @SerialName("visibility_condition")
    public val visibilityCondition: Condition? = null,
    @SerialName("availability_condition")
    public val availabilityCondition: Condition? = null,
    public val effects: List<Effect> = emptyList(),
    @SerialName("next_scene")
    public val nextScene: SceneId,
) {
    public companion object {
        /**
         * Sentinel `nextScene` value for "the scene where this template
         * is applied".
         *
         * Use this **only** on a `ChoiceTemplate`. `applyTemplate`
         * resolves it from its `currentSceneId` argument (required for
         * templates that use `@self`; throws `IllegalArgumentException`
         * if absent). Non-template `Choice` with `next_scene: "@self"`
         * is a dangling reference — `@self` is a template marker, not a
         * scene id.
         *
         * `@` is stripped by the editor's `transliterate`, so no real
         * scene id can collide with `@self`.
         */
        public val SELF: SceneId = SceneId("@self")
    }
}

FILE: engine/src/main/kotlin/com/myapp/adventure/engine/ir/Condition.kt
================================================
package com.myapp.adventure.engine.ir

import com.myapp.adventure.engine.ir.types.VarType
import kotlinx.serialization.SerialName
import kotlinx.serialization.Serializable

/**
 * AST of a condition that gates a choice, a scene, or an invariant.
 *
 * In `:app/data/Adventure.kt` conditions are plain strings
 * (`"has_sword"`, `"health >= 50"`). In the IR they are a typed tree:
 * the string is parsed once in `JsonToIr` (Ф1.3), and every consumer
 * (`evaluator` in Ф3, `Analyzer` in Ф1.6, future JS runtime in E1)
 * works with this tree instead of re-parsing strings.
 *
 * **Added in Ф3.1:** [Literal] and [VarRef] — both for forward use by
 * Ф3.2 (N7.base, `&&` / `||` / `!`), not yet produced by the parser.
 * The parser (`ConditionParser`) intentionally rejects a bare
 * `"health"` today with `ConditionError` — "not a valid condition".
 * When Ф3.2 extends the grammar to accept `A && B` (where `B` is a
 * bare variable reference), the parser will produce
 * `VarRef("B")`. Until then, these nodes can only appear in hand-built
 * IR (tests, future tooling). The writer (`ConditionWriter`, Ф3.1.2)
 * already covers them; the reader's `Evaluator` does too.
 */
@Serializable
public sealed class Condition {

    /**
     * A boolean literal: `true` or `false`.
     *
     * **Not produced by the parser yet.** There is no JSON syntax for a
     * literal condition today — an author writes an empty
     * `"condition"` field to mean "always true", not `"true"`. This node
     * exists for two future needs:
     *
     * 1. **AST optimizations** in Ф3.2 (`true && X` → `X`,
     *    `false || X` → `X`) — the optimizer produces `Literal` as an
     *    intermediate or final form.
     * 2. **Round-trip completeness** in `ConditionWriter` (Ф3.1.2):
     *    the writer must handle every sealed variant; a missing variant
     *    would make the `when` non-exhaustive.
     *
     * Evaluated by `Evaluator.evaluate` as its [value].
     */
    @Serializable
    @SerialName("literal")
    public data class Literal(
        public val value: Boolean,
    ) : Condition()

    /**
     * A bare reference to a variable: `VarRef("has_sword")`.
     *
     * Semantically reads the same as `Has("has_sword")` for Bool
     * variables — "is this Bool true?". The reason for a separate node
     * is **syntax** in the future `&&` / `||` grammar (Ф3.2): when the
     * author writes `has_sword && health_check_passed`, the second
     * operand is a bare variable reference (`health_check_passed`),
     * not a `has_X` condition. Without `VarRef`, the parser would have
     * to invent a `Has` wrapper, which loses the syntactic distinction
     * and makes the writer emit `has_health_check_passed` — a different
     * string.
     *
     * **Not produced by the parser yet.** A bare `"health"` in JSON is
     * a parse error (`ConditionParser` returns `ConditionError` with
     * "not a valid condition"). This is **intentional** until Ф3.2:
     * accepting it today would silently treat a typo (`"helth"`) as
     * `VarRef("helth")` instead of rejecting the malformed condition.
     *
     * **Evaluator** handles this by reading `state.flags.contains(name)`
     * (same as `Has`). **Type checker** treats it as no-op in Ф3.1 —
     * `VarRef` is not produced by the parser, so there is nothing to
     * check in practice; Ф3.2 will add `VarRefOnNonBool` when the parser
     * starts producing the node.
     */
    @Serializable
    @SerialName("var_ref")
    public data class VarRef(
        public val name: String,
    ) : Condition()

    /**
     * `has_X` — true if boolean flag `X` is set.
     *
     * **Only for [VarType.Bool] variables.** For numeric variables
     * ([VarType.Integer], [VarType.IntRange], [VarType.ItemCount]) use
     * [Compare] instead: `sword > 0` rather than `has_sword`,
     * `health > 0` rather than `has_health`. The type checker (Ф2.2)
     * rejects `Has` on non-boolean variables with a hint to use [Compare].
     *
     * The parser (Ф1.3) does **not** enforce this — it is a pure
     * syntactic transformation `"has_X"` → `Has("X")` and knows nothing
     * about variable types. Type checking is the single responsibility of
     * Ф2.2, which keeps parser and type checker decoupled.
     */
    @Serializable
    @SerialName("has")
    public data class Has(
        public val name: String,
    ) : Condition()

    /** `!X` — logical negation of [inner]. */
    @Serializable
    @SerialName("not")
    public data class Not(
        public val inner: Condition,
    ) : Condition()

    /** `X && Y` — logical conjunction. Short-circuits left to right. */
    @Serializable
    @SerialName("and")
    public data class And(
        public val left: Condition,
        public val right: Condition,
    ) : Condition()

    /** `X || Y` — logical disjunction. Short-circuits left to right. */
    @Serializable
    @SerialName("or")
    public data class Or(
        public val left: Condition,
        public val right: Condition,
    ) : Condition()

    /**
     * `X <op> N` — comparison of variable [varName] against integer [value].
     *
     * `varName` must resolve to [VarType.Integer] or [VarType.IntRange];
     * anything else is a type error (Ф2). [CompareOp] determines the operator.
     */
    @Serializable
    @SerialName("compare")
    public data class Compare(
        @SerialName("var_name")
        public val varName: String,
        public val op: CompareOp,
        public val value: Int,
    ) : Condition()

    /**
     * `X in min..max` — inclusive range check for variable [varName].
     *
     * `varName` must resolve to [VarType.IntRange] (or [VarType.Integer]
     * when `min..max` is inside `IntRange` bounds); checked in Ф2.
     */
    @Serializable
    @SerialName("in_range")
    public data class InRange(
        @SerialName("var_name")
        public val varName: String,
        public val min: Int,
        public val max: Int,
    ) : Condition()
}

package com.myapp.adventure.engine.ir

import kotlinx.serialization.SerialName
import kotlinx.serialization.Serializable

/**
 * Describes how the player dies and what recovery options they get.
 *
 * Corresponds to `:app/data/Adventure.kt`'s `DeathScene`.
 *
 * **Not a real [Scene].** The death screen is not part of the chapter
 * sequence: it is shown when the player's `health` reaches zero (or another
 * death invariant fires — see Ф3.5). Modelling it as a separate class keeps
 * [Chapter.scenes] clean of pseudo-scenes that would confuse the analyzer
 * (reachability, chapter grouping).
 *
 * **Default id.** If the adventure file omits `death_scene.id`, the parser
 * (Ф1.3) uses `"death_scene"`, matching
 * `AdventureEditorViewModel.buildAdventure()`.
 *
 * **All three `allow*` flags default to `true`.** The current
 * `DeathScene` in `:app` has the same defaults; matching them keeps
 * `test_adventure.json` (which sets them explicitly) and adventures that
 * omit them behave identically.
 *
 * @property id scene-like identifier used by the reader for logging and
 *   for the "step back" mechanism.
 * @property text death message shown to the player.
 * @property allowStepBack whether the "step back" recovery button is shown.
 * @property allowChapterRestart whether the "restart chapter" button is shown.
 * @property allowAdventureRestart whether the "restart adventure" button is shown.
 */
@Serializable
public data class DeathScene(
    public val id: SceneId = SceneId("death_scene"),
    /**
     * Ф4-infra (3b-6h): empty default, not `"💀 Вы погибли."`. The RU
     * default used to live in the IR; that made the engine a hidden
     * source of user-facing text. Now the reader falls back to
     * `R.string.reader_default_death_text` when this is empty. See
     * `i18n-policy.md` — data defaults in `:engine` must not carry
     * RU text; user-facing fallbacks live in `:app` resources.
     */
    public val text: String = "",
    @SerialName("allow_step_back")
    public val allowStepBack: Boolean = true,
    @SerialName("allow_chapter_restart")
    public val allowChapterRestart: Boolean = true,
    @SerialName("allow_adventure_restart")
    public val allowAdventureRestart: Boolean = true,
)

FILE: engine/src/main/kotlin/com/myapp/adventure/engine/ir/Effect.kt
================================================
package com.myapp.adventure.engine.ir

import kotlinx.serialization.SerialName
import kotlinx.serialization.Serializable

/**
 * A single state-modifying effect attached to a [Scene] or [Choice].
 *
 * In `:app/data/Adventure.kt` effects are three parallel nullable fields
 * (`set_flags`, `remove_flags`, `modify_stats`). In the IR each individual
 * change is one [Effect], and the parser (Ф1.3) turns the three fields into
 * a flat `List<Effect>`. Runtime applies effects in declaration order
 * (Ф1.5), so reordering affects semantics — that is intentional and
 * matches the current reader behaviour.
 *
 * Effects are **applied once** when a scene is first entered or when a
 * choice is picked. See `AdventureReaderFragment.applyEffects` for the
 * reference semantics.
 *
 * **Added in Ф3.1:** [Set] — set a stat to an absolute value. Not
 * produced by the parser today (the adventure JSON format has no field
 * for absolute set; `"modify_stats"` is delta-only). Runtime
 * (`EffectsApplier`) and type checker (`TypeChecker`) already handle it,
 * so it can appear in hand-built IR (tests, future tooling) without any
 * "unsupported effect" branch. Ф8 (`IrToJson`) will decide whether to
 * add a JSON field for it.
 */
@Serializable
public sealed class Effect {

    /**
     * `set_flags` entry: add [name] to the player's flag set (if not
     * already present). Idempotent.
     *
     * Only meaningful for [TagCategory.JOURNAL] tags; the type checker (Ф2)
     * will reject `set_flags` on `ITEM`/`HEALTH` tags.
     */
    @Serializable
    @SerialName("set_flag")
    public data class SetFlag(
        public val name: String,
    ) : Effect()

    /**
     * `remove_flags` entry: remove [name] from the player's flag set
     * (if present). Idempotent.
     *
     * Only meaningful for [TagCategory.JOURNAL] tags; `ITEM`/`HEALTH`
     * tags are removed by setting their value to zero via [ModifyStat]
     * or [Set].
     */
    @Serializable
    @SerialName("remove_flag")
    public data class RemoveFlag(
        public val name: String,
    ) : Effect()

    /**
     * `modify_stats` entry: add [delta] to the current value of [name].
     *
     * **Delta semantics, not absolute.** If the current value is `10` and
     * `delta` is `-3`, the new value is `7`. This matches the current
     * `AdventureReaderFragment.applyEffects`.
     *
     * For [TagCategory.HEALTH] and [TagCategory.ITEM] variables the result
     * is clamped to `>= 0` (current behaviour). For [TagCategory.JOURNAL]
     * numeric values there is no clamping. Clamping policy lives in the
     * runtime (Ф1.5), not here — [Effect] is a pure data description.
     */
    @Serializable
    @SerialName("modify_stat")
    public data class ModifyStat(
        public val name: String,
        public val delta: Int,
    ) : Effect()

    /**
     * Set [name] to [value] (absolute, not delta).
     *
     * **Difference from [ModifyStat].** `ModifyStat(name, -5)` means
     * "subtract 5"; `Set(name, 0)` means "reset to 0 regardless of the
     * current value". Authors use `Set` when they do not (or cannot)
     * know the current value — e.g. "health is restored to 100" in a
     * shrine scene, regardless of how wounded the player is.
     *
     * **Not produced by the parser today.** The adventure JSON format
     * (`"modify_stats": {"name": delta}`) does not have a syntax for
     * absolute set. This node exists for two reasons:
     *
     * 1. **Completeness of the effect model** — `Set` is a distinct
     *    semantic operation, and modelling it now (with runtime + type
     *    checker support) means Ф8 (`IrToJson`) can add a JSON field
     *    for it without touching every consumer of `Effect`.
     * 2. **Hand-built IR and tests** — `EngineStepTest`, the future
     *    editor "Suggest effect" tooling (Ф9.2), and any tool that
     *    constructs `Adventure` programmatically can emit `Set` and
     *    get the correct behaviour without an "unsupported effect"
     *    branch.
     *
     * **Runtime clamp.** Like [ModifyStat], the runtime clamps the
     * result to `>= 0` today (same policy — see `EffectsApplier` KDoc).
     * Type-aware clamping lands in Ф5.
     *
     * **Type checking.** Requires a numeric variable — `Bool` and
     * `ItemList` are rejected with [com.myapp.adventure.engine.ir.types.TypeError.ModifyStatOnNonNumeric]
     * (same variant as [ModifyStat] — the error is "numeric operation on
     * a non-numeric variable", the distinction between `Set` and
     * `ModifyStat` is not the point).
     */
    @Serializable
    @SerialName("set")
    public data class Set(
        public val name: String,
        public val value: Int,
    ) : Effect()
}

FILE: engine/src/main/kotlin/com/myapp/adventure/engine/ir/Gate.kt
================================================
package com.myapp.adventure.engine.ir

import kotlinx.serialization.SerialName
import kotlinx.serialization.Serializable

/**
 * A step gate on a [Scene]: the player must walk at least [requiredSteps]
 * real-world steps after entering this scene before any exit is allowed
 * (picking a choice, or auto-advancing to the next scene/chapter).
 *
 * **Where gates live.** A gate belongs to the **scene it gates the exit
 * of**, not to the chapter it opens. A chapter is pure narrative
 * grouping; a gate is a mechanical requirement on a single scene. A gate
 * may sit anywhere in a chapter, several gates may sit in one chapter,
 * and a chapter may have none.
 *
 * **Two modes** ([repeatable]):
 *
 * - **`repeatable = false` (default).** "Once walked, always open **in
 *   this playthrough**". The gate blocks the first time the player
 *   enters the scene; after [requiredSteps] are accumulated, the gate is
 *   marked as passed for this playthrough and **does not re-engage** if
 *   the player returns to this scene. Resetting the adventure
 *   (`restart`) clears the pass. Use this for the common case: "walk
 *   N steps to unlock the next chapter" — once unlocked, the player
 *   never re-walks.
 * - **`repeatable = true`.** Per-visit. Each time the player enters
 *   this scene (including by picking a choice that self-loops back to
 *   it), they must walk [requiredSteps] again. Use this for the
 *   "travelled a path" case: the player physically walks from location
 *   A to location B; returning to A and travelling to B again requires
 *   the same walk. Also useful for time-gated scenes: "you must wait
 *   N steps before you can pick anything here" — every visit.
 *
 * The author picks the mode in the editor. Default is `false` because
 * the "re-walked" surprise is worse than "unlocked but stays unlocked":
 * a player who unlocked a chapter once does not expect to unlock it
 * again by accident.
 *
 * **In JSON (adventure file format)** the gate is a flat pair:
 * `"gate": 4000` (required steps) and, optionally,
 * `"gate_repeatable": true`. `gate_repeatable` defaults to `false`, so
 * simple gates stay one-key.
 *
 * **In the IR** `Gate` is a data class with two fields
 * ([requiredSteps] and [repeatable]). The reason it is not a
 * `value class` anymore: `value class` requires exactly one field, and
 * we need two. IR serialization therefore wraps the gate as
 * `{"required_steps": N, "repeatable": bool}`. This is **IR
 * serialization**, not adventure file format — the two are different
 * by design (`golden_ir.json` is IR, not adventure).
 *
 * **Positive by construction.** `requiredSteps <= 0` is meaningless
 * ("walk at least 0 steps" = "no gate"). The parser (`JsonToIr`)
 * rejects `gate <= 0` as a structural error; `Gate(0)` should never be
 * constructed. "No gate" is `Scene.gate == null`.
 *
 * **Not checked by `Engine.step`.** Step counting is a reader concern
 * (a foreground service in `:app`). The engine does not know how many
 * steps the player has walked, nor whether a gate was already passed;
 * it only knows the mechanical shape of the gate. The reader checks the
 * gate, tracks which gates have been passed (per playthrough for
 * `repeatable = false`, per-visit for `repeatable = true`), and only
 * calls `Engine.step` when the current gate is open. This keeps the
 * engine free of wall-clock and sensor dependencies.
 *
 * @property requiredSteps number of steps to accumulate before the
 *   scene becomes exitable. Must be strictly positive.
 * @property repeatable whether the gate re-engages on every visit
 *   (`true`) or once passed stays passed for this playthrough
 *   (`false`, default).
 */
@Serializable
public data class Gate(
    @SerialName("required_steps")
    public val requiredSteps: Int,
    public val repeatable: Boolean = false,
)

package com.myapp.adventure.engine.ir

import com.myapp.adventure.engine.ir.types.VarDecl
import com.myapp.adventure.engine.ir.types.VarType
import kotlinx.serialization.Serializable

/**
 * Player state at the very start of an adventure, before the first scene
 * is entered.
 *
 * Corresponds to `:app/data/Adventure.kt`'s `PlayerState`, with one
 * difference: [flags] and [stats] are non-null with empty defaults, not
 * nullable. Nullable collections force every consumer to write
 * `?: emptyList()` at each call site; the IR instead says "no flags" as
 * `emptyList()`. The parser (Ф1.3) maps JSON's absent `null` / missing
 * fields to those defaults.
 *
 * **Precedence against [VarDecl]:** if a variable is declared in
 * [Adventure.variables] but not listed in [flags] / [stats], its value is
 * the type's default (see [VarType] KDoc). If listed, the value here wins.
 * This is the same as the current reader's `initNormalState()` behaviour.
 *
 * **Type consistency:** every flag / stat name here must be declared in
 * [Adventure.variables] — enforced by the type checker in Ф2.
 *
 * @property flags flags the player starts with.
 * @property stats numeric values the player starts with.
 */
@Serializable
public data class InitialState(
    public val flags: List<String> = emptyList(),
    public val stats: Map<String, Int> = emptyMap(),
)

FILE: engine/src/main/kotlin/com/myapp/adventure/engine/ir/Invariant.kt
================================================
package com.myapp.adventure.engine.ir

import kotlinx.serialization.Serializable

/**
 * A global rule that fires whenever its [condition] holds, regardless
 * of which scene the player is in.
 *
 * **Semantics** (Ф3.5, N2):
 *
 * > `Invariant(condition, outcome)` — evaluated **after every step**
 * > (choice pick + scene entry). If `condition` holds, `outcome` is
 * > applied immediately.
 *
 * The canonical example is `Invariant(Compare("health", LE, 0),
 * Outcome.Death)`: whenever the player's health is zero or below,
 * they die — no matter which scene's `modify_stats` pushed it there.
 *
 * **Where the invariants are checked.** `Engine.evaluateInvariants`
 * (Ф3.5.2), called by `Engine.step` after applying choice effects and
 * by the reader after applying scene effects. Whichever path first
 * brings the player into a violated state, the outcome fires there.
 *
 * **Fallback when `Adventure.invariants` is empty.** To preserve
 * behaviour for pre-Ф3.5 files (which have no `invariants` field),
 * `Engine.evaluateInvariants` falls back to the hardcoded
 * `health <= 0 => Death` rule (see `Evaluator.isDead`). A file with a
 * non-empty `invariants` list **replaces** the fallback entirely — if
 * the author wants health-death plus another rule, they declare both.
 *
 * **Why per-invariant outcomes, not a single `Outcome` for the
 * whole list.** The list is heterogeneous: `Invariant(health <= 0,
 * Death)` and (in a future phase) `Invariant(roll(1d6) == 1,
 * Custom("teleport"))` coexist. The `Outcome` belongs to the rule
 * that fires.
 *
 * **Determinism.** `Engine.evaluateInvariants` returns the outcome of
 * the **first** matching invariant, in list order. An author who
 * declares `[A, B]` where both hold at the same time sees `A`'s
 * outcome — the "specific rules first, generic rules last" pattern is
 * the author's responsibility (same as in `Guard`-style systems).
 *
 * **Serialized** as `{"condition": <Condition AST>, "outcome": <Outcome>}`.
 * In the adventure file format (`JsonToIr` reads / `:app` writes) the
 * condition is a plain string and the outcome is a flat string — see
 * `InvariantDto`.
 *
 * @property condition evaluated after every step. When it holds,
 *   [outcome] fires.
 * @property outcome what fires. Today the only variant is
 *   [Outcome.Death].
 */
@Serializable
public data class Invariant(
    public val condition: Condition,
    public val outcome: Outcome,
)


================================================
FILE: engine/src/main/kotlin/com/myapp/adventure/engine/ir/Outcome.kt
================================================
package com.myapp.adventure.engine.ir

import kotlinx.serialization.SerialName
import kotlinx.serialization.Serializable

/**
 * What happens when an [Invariant]'s condition fires.
 *
 * **One variant today: [Death].** The player dies, the reader shows
 * the death screen (`Adventure.deathScene` if present, else the
 * built-in default), and the usual death-screen choices (step back /
 * chapter restart / adventure restart) apply — exactly as if
 * `health <= 0` had fired under the pre-Ф3.5 hardcoded rule.
 *
 * **Why a sealed class, not an enum.** A future variant
 * `Custom(name: String)` (Ф12/Ф13: "if `roll(1d6) == 1`, jump to scene
 * `X`") carries data. A sealed class absorbs that without breaking
 * `when (outcome)` callers; an enum would force a parallel map from
 * enum value to data. One variant is fine to start with — the sealed
 * class grows additively.
 *
 * **Why not `Ending` as a second variant today.** "Win the game" is
 * already expressed by `Scene.isEnding = true` — the reader shows the
 * "the end" screen, no death, no rollback. Adding `Outcome.Ending`
 * would create two mechanisms for the same player outcome and make it
 * ambiguous which one wins when both apply. If a future feature needs
 * an invariant that ends the adventure **at the current scene** with
 * a different flavour ("you retire rich"), it will arrive as
 * `Outcome.Ending(sceneId)` — a dedicated jump, not a synonym for
 * `Scene.isEnding`.
 *
 * **Serialized** as `{"type": "death"}` in IR JSON (polymorphic
 * envelope from `kotlinx.serialization`). In the adventure file
 * format (`:app` writes / `JsonToIr` reads) the outcome is a flat
 * string `"outcome": "death"` — see `InvariantDto` in
 * `engine/.../format/dto/Dto.kt`. The two shapes differ on purpose:
 * IR is an internal cache, adventure JSON is what the author sees.
 */
@Serializable
public sealed class Outcome {

    /**
     * The player dies. The reader shows the death screen
     * ([Adventure.deathScene] if present, else the built-in default
     * "💀 Вы погибли."), and the usual recovery options apply
     * (see [DeathScene.allowStepBack] and siblings).
     *
     * Semantically identical to the pre-Ф3.5 hardcoded
     * `health <= 0 => death` rule: when `Invariant(health <= 0,
     * Death)` is present, the behaviour is byte-for-byte the same as
     * before. The advantage: the author can add **more** invariants
     * (`stamina <= 0`, `has_poison && health < 50`, …) without
     * changing the engine.
     */
    @Serializable
    @SerialName("death")
    public data object Death : Outcome()
}

FILE: engine/src/main/kotlin/com/myapp/adventure/engine/ir/PlayerState.kt
================================================
package com.myapp.adventure.engine.ir

import com.myapp.adventure.engine.ir.types.VarType

/**
 * Player state during an adventure: what the player has right now.
 *
 * **Immutable.** Every change produces a new instance via [copy]. This
 * makes three things trivial that would otherwise be error-prone:
 *
 * 1. **Undo / "step back" after death.** Snapshot the state before the
 *    step; restoring it is `state = savedState`, no deep copy, no
 *    rollback logic. Already used by the reader
 *    (`previousStepSnapshot`, `chapterStartSnapshot`).
 * 2. **Save / load.** A state is a value; serializing it (Ф5/S5) is
 *    straightforward. Snapshots can be compared with `==`.
 * 3. **Unit testing.** `applyEffects(state, effects)` returns a new state;
 *    no shared mutable state between tests, no setup/teardown.
 *
 * The cost — one allocation per change — is negligible in the reader:
 * at most one change per user tap. The editor does not use
 * [PlayerState] at all (it works with `EditorModels`).
 *
 * **Distinct from [InitialState].**
 * - [InitialState] is part of the adventure data: "with what flags/stats
 *   does the player start". Serialized in JSON.
 * - [PlayerState] is runtime state: "where the player is now". Never
 *   serialized as part of [Adventure]; persists via the separate progress
 *   file (Ф5/S5).
 *
 * The reader creates a `PlayerState` from an `InitialState` at adventure
 * start; the analyzer (Ф1.6) uses both to reason about reachable states.
 *
 * **Flags vs stats.**
 * - [flags] — boolean markers ("visited_forest", "knows_secret").
 * - [stats] — numeric values ("health" = 100, "gold" = 5).
 *
 * Which side a variable lives on is determined by its declared type
 * ([VarType.Bool] → [flags]; anything numeric → [stats]). If the same
 * name appears in both, the analyzer reports it — either the author has
 * a genuine naming collision or the type checker (Ф2) will catch it.
 *
 * **No clamping here.** This class is a pure value: it does not enforce
 * that "health" stays non-negative. That policy lives in `Engine.applyEffects`
 * (Ф1.5), because clamping depends on the variable's declared type
 * (`HEALTH`/`ITEM` → `>= 0` after Ф2.8; unbounded for `Integer`). Keeping
 * the policy out of the data type keeps [PlayerState] reusable across
 * reader, analyzer, and any future UI preview.
 *
 * @property flags boolean flags currently true.
 * @property stats numeric values currently held.
 */
public data class PlayerState(
    public val flags: Set<String> = emptySet(),
    public val stats: Map<String, Int> = emptyMap(),
)

/**
 * Creates a [PlayerState] from the adventure's [InitialState].
 *
 * The reader calls this once at adventure start (and on "restart
 * adventure") to build the first [PlayerState] from the JSON-declared
 * starting flags/stats. The engine does not depend on this function:
 * `Engine.step` always takes a [PlayerState], never an [InitialState].
 *
 * Collections are copied (`toSet`/`toMap`) so the [PlayerState] does not
 * alias the [InitialState] lists. Immutability is the whole point of
 * [PlayerState]; sharing a mutable backing would break that invariant.
 */
public fun InitialState.toPlayerState(): PlayerState =
    PlayerState(flags = flags.toSet(), stats = stats.toMap())

FILE: engine/src/main/kotlin/com/myapp/adventure/engine/ir/Scene.kt
================================================
package com.myapp.adventure.engine.ir

import kotlinx.serialization.SerialName
import kotlinx.serialization.Serializable

/**
 * One screen of an adventure: body text, optional effects, and (optionally)
 * a list of [Choice]s the player can pick.
 *
 * Corresponds to `:app/data/Adventure.kt`'s `Scene`, with two differences:
 *
 * 1. The three JSON fields `set_flags`, `remove_flags`, `modify_stats` are
 *    flattened into [effects] (see [Effect]). Order is preserved by the
 *    parser (Ф1.3): `set_flags` first, then `remove_flags`, then
 *    `modify_stats`, matching the current reader's `applyEffects`.
 * 2. Scenes are grouped into [Chapter]s. There is no `isChapterEnd` flag in
 *    the IR: chapter boundaries are the boundaries of [Chapter.scenes].
 *
 * **A scene with no [choices]** is a terminal scene: the story **must**
 * mark it with [isEnding] = `true`, or the analyzer reports
 * [com.myapp.adventure.engine.analyze.LintKind.DeadEnd] (severity
 * `ERROR`). The reader does **not** guess: it never auto-advances to the
 * next chapter. "End of chapter" must be expressed by an explicit
 * Continue-choice that leads to the first scene of the next chapter.
 *
 * @property id unique scene identifier within an adventure.
 * @property text body text shown to the player.
 * @property effects state changes applied the first time the scene is
 *   entered, in order. Re-entering a scene does not re-apply them.
 * @property choices actions shown below the text; may be empty.
 * @property gate optional step gate: the player must walk
 *   [Gate.requiredSteps] steps **after entering this scene** before any
 *   exit is allowed. `null` means "no gate". Gates are independent of
 *   chapters — a chapter may have zero, one, or many gated scenes, and a
 *   gated scene may sit anywhere in a chapter. See [Gate] for details.
 * @property isEnding whether this scene ends the adventure. Multiple
 *   scenes in the same adventure may be marked `true` — that is how
 *   authors model multiple endings ("win" / "die" / "retire rich" /
 *   etc.). A scene marked `true` **must** have no [choices] — the reader
 *   would otherwise render buttons that lead nowhere. Marking a scene
 *   with [isEnding] = `true` **and** non-empty [choices] is reported by
 *   [com.myapp.adventure.engine.analyze.LintKind.EndingSceneWithChoices]
 *   (severity `ERROR`). Defaults to `false`; this matches the
 *   pre-`isEnding` behaviour, where "no choices" silently meant "end".
 *
 * **Not to be confused with [DeathScene].** `DeathScene` is not part of
 * [Chapter.scenes] and does not carry [isEnding]. A scene marked
 * [isEnding] = `true` describes an *authored* ending ("you win", "you
 * retire"); the death screen is shown automatically when the player's
 * `health` reaches `0` and is **not** one of the scenes.
 */
@Serializable
public data class Scene(
    public val id: SceneId,
    public val text: String,
    public val effects: List<Effect> = emptyList(),
    public val choices: List<Choice> = emptyList(),
    public val gate: Gate? = null,
    @SerialName("is_ending")
    public val isEnding: Boolean = false,
    /**
     * Ф4.5 (N5): this scene is a **merge point** — a deliberate convergence
     * of two or more narrative branches. The field is metadata: it does
     * **not** change runtime behaviour (a merge point is an ordinary
     * scene; entering it via `Engine.step` applies the incoming choice's
     * effects as usual, and subsequent steps see the accumulated state).
     *
     * **Why the metadata then?** The analyzer (Ф4.6) will use it to
     * verify "all declared source branches are actually reachable and
     * lead here" — unreachable or inconsistent merges are author
     * mistakes. It also lets the editor's map view (Ф4.10) render a
     * visual join. Without the marker, a merge point is
     * indistinguishable from an ordinary scene that happens to have
     * multiple incoming edges.
     *
     * **Delta semantics (Ф4.5 decision C1).** "Merge transfers the
     * delta" is satisfied **implicitly**: each branch applies its own
     * `choice.effects` (and `scene.effects`, once per first entry)
     * before entering the merge scene; `PlayerState` arriving at the
     * merge is the sum of those deltas on top of the pre-branch state.
     * There is **no** runtime "merge delta" application — the current
     * model does not track per-branch deltas separately from the state.
     * The `merge: true` flag is a *declaration* that this scene is where
     * branches converge, not a runtime operation.
     */
    @SerialName("merge")
    public val isMerge: Boolean = false,
    /**
     * Ф4.5 (N5): declared source branches — scene ids that the author
     * says lead into this merge point. Optional even when [isMerge] is
     * `true`: if empty, the analyzer (Ф4.6) will collect incoming edges
     * from the `nextScene` graph. If non-empty, each id must exist —
     * [com.myapp.adventure.engine.CompileError.MissingMergeSource]
     * otherwise.
     *
     * The declaration is what makes the merge *explicit*: a plain scene
     * with two incoming choices is an *implicit* merge; a scene with
     * `merge: true` + `mergeSources` declares "these are the branches I
     * intended to join here", which the analyzer can then validate.
     */
    @SerialName("merge_sources")
    public val mergeSources: List<SceneId> = emptyList(),
)

package com.myapp.adventure.engine.ir

import kotlinx.serialization.Serializable
import kotlin.jvm.JvmInline

/**
 * Stable identifier of a scene within an adventure.
 *
 * Wraps a [String] so that `Choice.nextScene` (a scene reference) cannot be
 * accidentally confused with a flag name, a stat name, or any other plain
 * string. Zero runtime cost — `@JvmInline value class` is erased to the
 * underlying `String` on JVM.
 *
 * **Serialized transparently** as the underlying string. `SceneId("start")`
 * appears in JSON as `"start"`, not as `{"value":"start"}`. This is what
 * `kotlinx.serialization` does for `@JvmInline value class` by default and
 * matches the current adventure file format.
 *
 * **Uniqueness** is enforced by the type checker (Ф2), not by the type
 * itself: two scenes could still be constructed with the same `SceneId`.
 *
 * Other IDs (`ChoiceId`, `ChapterId`, `VariableName`) are intentionally
 * plain `String` for now — a `SceneId` is the most frequent source of
 * confusion (`nextScene` vs a flag/stat name), so it gets the strongest
 * typing. Add value classes to the others only if the same confusion
 * materializes there.
 */
@Serializable
@JvmInline
public value class SceneId(public val value: String)

FILE: engine/src/main/kotlin/com/myapp/adventure/engine/ir/Subroutine.kt
================================================
package com.myapp.adventure.engine.ir

import com.myapp.adventure.engine.ir.types.VarDecl
import kotlinx.serialization.SerialName
import kotlinx.serialization.Serializable

/**
 * Ф4.7 (N6.base): a reusable, atomic procedure.
 *
 * **Atomic by design.** A subroutine runs to completion inside a single
 * [com.myapp.adventure.engine.Engine.step] call; the player never sees
 * intermediate screens or choices. This is what keeps the reader fast and
 * the save format unchanged: there is no persisted call stack, no
 * mid-subroutine save, and undo returns to the state before the choice
 * that invoked the subroutine. Player-visible multi-step content belongs
 * to reusable scenes (a separate feature), not here.
 *
 * **Local frame (decision A1 of Ф4.7).** A call creates a private frame:
 * - [inputs] are copied **into** the frame from the caller before the body
 *   starts. Inside the frame these names are read-only.
 * - [outputs] are initialised to their type defaults, may be written by the
 *   body, and are copied **out** to the caller's target variables when the
 *   frame returns. A name that appears in both [inputs] and [outputs] is an
 *   in-out parameter: it starts with the caller's value and is written back
 *   on return (the types must match; checked by the parser/type checker).
 * - The body can access **only** these local names. It cannot read or
 *   mutate global `Adventure.variables` directly; anything the procedure
 *   needs must be passed as an input, and anything it changes must be
 *   exposed as an output. This is what makes a subroutine a predictable
 *   contract instead of a hidden side effect.
 *
 * **Nesting and the call stack.** A body step may [SubroutineStep.call]
 * another subroutine. The runtime keeps an explicit stack of frames, so a
 * callee's outputs can be written into the caller's locals and the caller
 * resumes at the next body step. Recursion and cycles are **not** allowed in
 * N6.base: `Engine.compile` rejects a cyclic call graph
 * ([com.myapp.adventure.engine.CompileError.SubroutineCycle]). Bounded loops
 * and local variables beyond parameters belong to Ф13 `Procedure`.
 *
 * **No version bump.** `Adventure.subroutines` is an optional list with an
 * empty default; identity migration, same reasoning as `variables` (Ф2.8),
 * `invariants` (Ф3.5), `choice_templates` (Ф4.1), `merge` (Ф4.5).
 *
 * @property id stable, machine-readable identifier (e.g. `"drink_potion"`).
 *   Unique within an adventure; checked by the parser.
 * @property inputs typed parameters copied into the frame before the body.
 *   Order is meaningful for documentation and for the editor's parameter
 *   list. Duplicate names are a structural error.
 * @property outputs typed parameters written back to the caller on return.
 *   May overlap [inputs] by name (in-out parameter), but the overlapping
 *   types must be identical.
 * @property body ordered steps executed top to bottom. Each step may be
 *   guarded by a [SubroutineStep.condition], apply effects, and/or call
 *   another subroutine.
 */
@Serializable
public data class Subroutine(
    public val id: String,
    public val inputs: List<VarDecl> = emptyList(),
    public val outputs: List<VarDecl> = emptyList(),
    public val body: List<SubroutineStep> = emptyList(),
)

/**
 * One step of a [Subroutine] body.
 *
 * **Execution order inside a step.** If [condition] is non-null and
 * evaluates to `false`, the step is skipped entirely. Otherwise [effects] are
 * applied to the current frame in list order, then [call] (if present) is
 * executed. A step with both effects and a call is the canonical
 * "consume the input, then run the shared logic" pattern.
 *
 * **Why a flat list of guarded steps, not a nested `if` tree.** The authoring
 * UI (Ф4.8) is a table: condition + effects + optional call per row. That is
 * easier to read and edit than a nested block editor, and it covers the same
 * finite branching: an `else` branch is a following step with the negated
 * condition. Loops and nested control flow are explicitly out of N6.base
 * (N6.advanced / Ф13).
 *
 * @property condition optional guard; `null` means "always run".
 * @property effects state changes applied to the frame, in order.
 * @property call optional nested subroutine call executed after [effects].
 */
@Serializable
public data class SubroutineStep(
    public val condition: Condition? = null,
    public val effects: List<Effect> = emptyList(),
    public val call: SubroutineCall? = null,
)

/**
 * A call to a [Subroutine], used either on a [Choice] (top-level call) or
 * inside a [SubroutineStep] (nested call).
 *
 * **Name resolution depends on context.**
 * - On a [Choice], [args] sources and [outputs] targets are names of
 *   **global** variables from `Adventure.variables`.
 * - Inside a subroutine body, they are names of **local** parameters of the
 *   enclosing frame ([Subroutine.inputs] / [Subroutine.outputs]).
 *
 * This is a small, deliberate scoping rule: nested calls compose local
 * frames; top-level calls connect frames to the player's state. It keeps the
 * runtime predictable and lets the type checker validate both directions.
 *
 * **Arguments and return values.**
 * - Every declared input must have an entry in [args]; extra entries are
 *   errors. The type of the source must match the parameter's declared type.
 * - [outputs] may cover a subset of the callee's outputs; an unmapped output
 *   is simply discarded. Extra target names are errors. The type of the
 *   target must match the output's declared type.
 * - Values are copied, never aliased: the callee starts with the current
 *   value of each source and writes its outputs back when it returns.
 *
 * @property subroutineId id of the callee; resolved by `Engine.compile`.
 * @property args callee input name → caller variable/local name.
 * @property outputs callee output name → caller variable/local name.
 */
@Serializable
public data class SubroutineCall(
    @SerialName("subroutine_id")
    public val subroutineId: String,
    public val args: Map<String, String> = emptyMap(),
    public val outputs: Map<String, String> = emptyMap(),
)

FILE: engine/src/main/kotlin/com/myapp/adventure/engine/ir/TemplateApplier.kt
================================================
package com.myapp.adventure.engine.ir

/**
 * Instantiates a [ChoiceTemplate] into a fully-expanded [Choice].
 *
 * **Design (Ф4.2 decision A1): expansion.** The returned [Choice] has
 * its `text`, `condition`, `visibilityCondition`, and `effects` filled
 * in with substituted values. The runtime (`Engine.step`,
 * `Evaluator`, `EffectsApplier`) and the analyzer see only expanded
 * choices; they never look at `Adventure.choiceTemplates` or
 * `Choice.templateRef`. The `templateRef` field on the result records
 * the source (for the editor, Ф4.3).
 *
 * **Substitution semantics (Ф4.2 decision B1).** Args are
 * `Map<String, String>` — parameter name → actual variable name.
 * Substitution is:
 * - **Text**: `{paramName}` placeholders in [ChoiceTemplate.text] are
 *   replaced with the corresponding arg value. Example:
 *   `"Use {itemId}"` + `args = {itemId: "potion"}` → `"Use potion"`.
 * - **AST name slots**: [Condition.Has], [Condition.VarRef],
 *   [Condition.Compare], [Condition.InRange], [Effect.SetFlag],
 *   [Effect.RemoveFlag], [Effect.ModifyStat], [Effect.Set] are
 *   checked for **exact** parameter-name matches. If the string equals
 *   a parameter name, it is replaced with the arg value; otherwise it
 *   is left as-is (a reference to a global variable).
 * - **Int slots are not parameterizable**: `value` / `delta` / `min` /
 *   `max` (all `Int`) are copied verbatim. Integer parameterization
 *   requires a placeholder syntax for ints and is out of scope.
 * - **`nextScene`**: normally copied verbatim. The sentinel value
 *   [ChoiceTemplate.SELF] (`SceneId("@self")`) resolves to the
 *   caller-supplied [currentSceneId] — "the scene where this template is
 *   applied". Used for "use item" / "drink potion" choices that apply
 *   effects in place. If a template uses `@self` and [currentSceneId]
 *   is `null`, [applyTemplate] throws (a caller that applies a `@self`
 *   template without scene context is a bug, not an author error).
 *
 * **Validation.** [applyTemplate] requires:
 * - every parameter name in `template.parameters` is a key in [args];
 * - `args` has no keys that are not parameters (catches typos early).
 * Missing or extra args throw [IllegalArgumentException]. If args are
 * built by the editor (Ф4.3) or the JSON parser (Ф4.3), validation is
 * a developer-facing invariant, not author-facing input.
 *
 * **Pure.** No I/O, no logging, no mutation of [template] or [args].
 *
 * @param template the template to instantiate.
 * @param args parameter name → actual variable name.
 * @param choiceId the id to assign to the resulting [Choice]. The
 *   caller owns id generation: the JSON parser (Ф4.3.3) will use
 *   `"${sceneId}_choice_${index}"`, the editor will use the same.
 * @param currentSceneId the scene where this template is being applied.
 *   Required if `template.nextScene == ChoiceTemplate.SELF`; ignored
 *   otherwise. The editor's "use template" flow (Ф4.3.2b) passes the
 *   parent scene's id here.
 * @return fully-expanded [Choice] with `templateRef` set.
 * @throws IllegalArgumentException if [args] does not match
 *   `template.parameters` (missing or extra keys).
 */
public fun applyTemplate(
    template: ChoiceTemplate,
    args: Map<String, String>,
    choiceId: ChoiceId,
    currentSceneId: SceneId? = null,
): Choice {
    val paramNames = template.parameters.map { it.name }.toSet()
    val missing = paramNames - args.keys
    require(missing.isEmpty()) {
        "Template '${template.id}': missing arguments for parameters $missing"
    }
    val extra = args.keys - paramNames
    require(extra.isEmpty()) {
        "Template '${template.id}': unexpected arguments (not in parameters): $extra"
    }
    return Choice(
        id = choiceId,
        text = substituteText(template.text, args),
        nextScene = resolveNextScene(template, currentSceneId),
        condition = template.availabilityCondition?.let {
            substituteCondition(it, args)
        },
        visibilityCondition = template.visibilityCondition?.let {
            substituteCondition(it, args)
        },
        effects = template.effects.map { substituteEffect(it, args) },
        templateRef = TemplateRef(template.id, args),
    )
}

/**
 * Convenience: looks up [templateId] in [Adventure.choiceTemplates] and
 * applies it. Returns `null` if the template is not found.
 *
 * Provided so that callers with only an [Adventure] in hand do not have
 * to write the lookup themselves. The core API is
 * [applyTemplate] with an explicit [ChoiceTemplate]; this overload is
 * sugar.
 */
public fun Adventure.applyTemplate(
    templateId: String,
    args: Map<String, String>,
    choiceId: ChoiceId,
    currentSceneId: SceneId? = null,
): Choice? {
    val template = choiceTemplates.firstOrNull { it.id == templateId } ?: return null
    return applyTemplate(template, args, choiceId, currentSceneId)
}

// ---------- Substitution helpers ----------

/**
 * Substitutes `{paramName}` placeholders in [text]. The `{...}` markers
 * make parameter references unambiguous: literal gamebook text is
 * unlikely to contain curly braces, and a bare name in text would be
 * indistinguishable from ordinary prose.
 */
private fun substituteText(text: String, args: Map<String, String>): String {
    if (args.isEmpty() || '{' !in text) return text
    var result = text
    for ((name, value) in args) {
        result = result.replace("{$name}", value)
    }
    return result
}

/**
 * Substitutes an **exact** parameter name in a name slot. Exact match
 * (no braces) is unambiguous here: a name slot contains either a
 * parameter name (substitute) or a global variable name (leave as-is).
 * Braces would be redundant and noisy in an AST.
 */
private fun substituteName(name: String, args: Map<String, String>): String =
    args[name] ?: name

private fun substituteCondition(
    condition: Condition,
    args: Map<String, String>,
): Condition = when (condition) {
    is Condition.Literal -> condition
    is Condition.VarRef -> Condition.VarRef(substituteName(condition.name, args))
    is Condition.Has -> Condition.Has(substituteName(condition.name, args))
    is Condition.Not -> Condition.Not(substituteCondition(condition.inner, args))
    is Condition.And -> Condition.And(
        substituteCondition(condition.left, args),
        substituteCondition(condition.right, args),
    )
    is Condition.Or -> Condition.Or(
        substituteCondition(condition.left, args),
        substituteCondition(condition.right, args),
    )
    is Condition.Compare -> Condition.Compare(
        varName = substituteName(condition.varName, args),
        op = condition.op,
        value = condition.value,
    )
    is Condition.InRange -> Condition.InRange(
        varName = substituteName(condition.varName, args),
        min = condition.min,
        max = condition.max,
    )
}

private fun substituteEffect(
    effect: Effect,
    args: Map<String, String>,
): Effect = when (effect) {
    is Effect.SetFlag -> Effect.SetFlag(substituteName(effect.name, args))
    is Effect.RemoveFlag -> Effect.RemoveFlag(substituteName(effect.name, args))
    is Effect.ModifyStat -> Effect.ModifyStat(substituteName(effect.name, args), effect.delta)
    is Effect.Set -> Effect.Set(substituteName(effect.name, args), effect.value)
}


/**
 * Resolves `template.nextScene` to the concrete scene id of the
 * resulting [Choice]:
 *
 * - normal `SceneId` → copied as-is;
 * - [ChoiceTemplate.SELF] → `currentSceneId` (required);
 * - `@self` without `currentSceneId` → [IllegalArgumentException].
 *
 * The exception is a **caller** error (misuse of the API), not an
 * author error: a template legitimately using `@self` requires the
 * caller to know the context. The editor (Ф4.3.2b) and the JSON parser
 * (Ф4.3.3) always know it; hand-written tests that do not use `@self`
 * never hit this branch.
 */
private fun resolveNextScene(
    template: ChoiceTemplate,
    currentSceneId: SceneId?,
): SceneId {
    if (template.nextScene != ChoiceTemplate.SELF) return template.nextScene
    return requireNotNull(currentSceneId) {
        "Template '${template.id}' uses @self, but no currentSceneId was provided. " +
                "Pass the scene id where this template is applied."
    }
}
